name: cache-aside
intent: Place the cache beside the authoritative store and make the application own the protocol: look up the cache first, load the entry from the store on a miss and populate it with a TTL, and invalidate the entry right after each write to the store - so repeated reads stay cheap while the store, never the cache, decides what is true.
problem: A source of truth (relational database, downstream service, object store) is expensive or rate-limited for the read volume an application receives, while most reads repeat a small set of keys: without a cache every request pays the source-of-truth cost, and with an unmanaged cache the copies silently drift. The recurring decision is where the read path looks first, when a miss may populate the entry, and what a write must do so the cached copy stops lying.
context: Read-heavy paths in front of a slower or metered authoritative store, typically several application instances sharing a Redis or Memcached tier, or each holding an in-process cache, where a bounded amount of staleness is acceptable and every writer can be held to the same invalidation discipline. It applies when the read/write ratio is high, when the cache itself does not provide read-through or write-through, and when lost or evicted entries can always be recomputed from the store.
benefits: Reads that hit the cache never touch the source of truth, so latency and load drop exactly on the paths that repeat.
Only requested data is cached: the working set tracks the real access pattern instead of preloading everything the application might need.
The cache can be added, resized or removed without changing the data model - the source of truth stays authoritative and the application keeps working (more slowly) with a cold or absent cache.
Failure isolation is explicit: a miss, an eviction or a cache outage is defined to fall back to the source of truth, so the cache never owns correctness.
Population policy (TTL, what to cache, what to skip) can be tuned per key family without touching the store or the callers.
tradeoffs: Bounded staleness is inherent: between a write to the source of truth and the invalidation or expiry of the entry, readers can see the previous value - and a writer that bypasses the application leaves the cache stale until the TTL fires.

The miss path is a load amplifier: a hot key that expires or is invalidated can send every concurrent reader to the source of truth at once, so stampede control (single-flight, per-key lock, early refresh) is part of the pattern rather than a later optimization.
Correctness depends on discipline repeated at every write path: commit to the store and only then invalidate - removing the entry first opens a window in which a reader repopulates the stale value.

The cache becomes a second production dependency with its own failure and capacity modes; if a cache outage is not degraded cleanly to the source of truth, the pattern turns an optimization into an availability risk.
Key structure, serialization format and their versioning become a contract: a deploy that changes the value shape can misread or overwrite entries unless keys carry a namespace or version.
Cold caches after a deploy or scale-out make the first requests slower exactly when traffic is rising, so priming or request coalescing has to be planned.
Tuning is per data set: too short a TTL thrashes the store, too long makes stale reads the norm, and eviction behaviour must be understood before the cache is trusted under pressure.

participants.responsibility: Asks the cache first and uses the source of truth only on a miss, so the lookup order is decided in one place instead of at every call site.
Keyed store of entries with an eviction policy and a TTL; may be in-process or shared, but never authoritative and never required for correctness.
The authoritative data store (database, service, object store) that is always correct and must remain able to answer when the cache cannot.
Reads the source of truth for the missing key, hands the value to the cache with an expiry, and decides what not to cache (errors, absent rows).
Commits changes to the source of truth and then removes or refreshes the corresponding entry; centralised so no writer can forget it.
Declares the TTL and the stale-read behaviour (serve stale, block, recompute) plus the stampede policy for hot keys that lapse.

use_cases: Read-heavy lookups by natural key (product catalogs, user profiles, article pages) in front of a relational database.
Several service instances sharing a Redis or Memcached tier where every instance must see the same cached copy and the same invalidation.
Reference data that changes slowly (currency rates, feature flags, configuration, price lists) refreshed by TTL with explicit invalidation when it is edited.
Expensive aggregate or derived results (dashboards, search pages, recommendations) recomputed into the cache per request key.
Per-instance in-process caches for hot, rarely changing values where a shared cache would add network latency without adding much.
Multi-level caching in Kubernetes: an in-process L1 (Caffeine) sidecar on each pod with an L2 Redis cluster, where the L1 is invalidated on each incoming request via a bloom filter or pub/sub.

CDN edge caching for static or semi-static API responses: the application server acts as the origin and issues cache-aside reads; CDN edges serve from their own look-aside cache with short TTLs and PURGE invalidation on writes.

RAG and vector cache in AI pipelines: embedding results cached by query hash so repeated semantically identical questions hit the vector store once and reuse cached results; TTL bounds staleness of the embedding index.

Django's low-level cache API (cache.get / cache.get_or_set with a per-key timeout, cache.delete on save) is cache-aside as a framework primitive; MediaWiki's WANObjectCache does the same at Wikipedia scale via getWithSet, invalidating page parses through cross-datacenter purges rather than direct writes.

Spring's cache abstraction applies the pattern declaratively: @Cacheable loads and populates on a miss, @CacheEvict removes the entry after the writer, with RedisCacheManager supplying the TTL - the application still owns both paths, the annotation only moves where.

Hibernate's second-level cache read-write concurrency strategy is a managed cache-aside: the updated entry is soft-locked around the transaction so concurrent readers miss to the database instead of repopulating the cache with the pre-commit value.
avoid_when: Read-after-write freshness is required on the same path: use write-through (or update the cache inside the same transaction) instead of tolerating a staleness window.
The data is static or small enough to hold in memory from startup: prime it once and serve it without a cache tier.
The cache or framework already provides read-through and write-through: do not re-implement the protocol underneath it.
The hit rate would be low because keys are mostly unique: the extra lookup and population work costs more than it saves.
The data is sensitive or security relevant and the cache is shared between users or applications: read it from the primary source instead.
anti_patterns: Cache-first writes: deleting or overwriting the entry before the source-of-truth commit, which lets a concurrent reader repopulate the stale value.
Cache as database: treating the cached copy as authoritative, so a flush or eviction becomes data loss.
No TTL and no invalidation on some write path: entries survive forever and the cache starts lying about the data.
Unbounded or unnamespaced caching of user-specific data in a shared cache, mixing tenants and leaking data across requests.
Expiring hot keys with no stampede protection, turning every expiry into a burst of duplicate source-of-truth reads.

Negative cache poisoning: if a key never existed in the source of truth and is not cached as absent, every request for it hits the origin; an attacker can enumerate non-existent IDs and saturate the database.

Hot-key saturation: a single key receiving orders-of-magnitude more QPS than median (e.g. a celebrity post) saturates one cache shard regardless of total cluster throughput; mitigate with key replication or an L1 buffer.

Cache penetration via key cardinality explosion: search queries, pagination and dynamic filters can create millions of unique keys with near-zero hit rate, thrashing the cache; cap key diversity and use a Bloom filter.

Serialization version skew: a deploy changes the value shape but old serialized entries are still in cache, causing deserialisation errors or silent data corruption; version keys with a schema prefix.

Double-write inconsistency: writing to cache and database in non-atomic sequence (cache-first, or database-write succeeds but cache-invalidate fails) leaves the cache and store disagreeing; always commit to the store first.
Cold cache after a rolling deploy: every new pod instance starts with an empty L1 in-process cache; without pre-warming the hot set, the first burst of traffic stampedes the shared L2 and origin.

Cache as a load-bearing dependency: if Redis going down causes the application to fail rather than degrade gracefully to the store, the cache has become a correctness dependency instead of an optimisation.
design_principles: Single source of truth: the cache is an optimization that may always be discarded, so correctness lives in the store.
Bounded staleness as an explicit contract: the TTL and the stale-read behaviour are part of the interface, not an accident.
Ordered write path: mutate the store first and invalidate second - the reverse order is a documented correctness bug.
Fail safe to the store: cache errors and evictions degrade to source-of-truth reads rather than wrong answers.
Centralised invalidation: one place defines which keys a write affects, so no writer can silently skip it.
best_practices: Update the source of truth first, then remove the entry (or refresh it); never invalidate before the commit.
Give every entry a TTL as a safety net even when explicit invalidation exists, and align it with how stale the data is allowed to be.
Namespace and version cache keys (application, schema version, tenant) so deploys and shared caches cannot misread each other.
Coalesce concurrent misses per key (single-flight, per-key lock, provider-side dedup) and consider serving briefly stale data while one loader refreshes.
Decide and document what is not cached: errors, missing rows (or a short negative entry), large objects, and anything sensitive.
Instrument hit ratio, miss latency and eviction behaviour; a cache that is not measured cannot be tuned or trusted.
Degrade explicitly: when the cache is unavailable, read the source of truth rather than failing the request.
Add TTL jitter (±10–20%) so entries filled together do not expire simultaneously, spreading the herd across time instead of concentrating it at the TTL cliff.
Cache negative results (the 'not found' sentinel) with a short TTL (30–60 s) to prevent cache-penetration attacks and reduce origin load from repeated absent-key queries.
Layer a local in-process L1 cache (e.g. Caffeine) in front of a shared L2 (Redis/Memcached) to reduce network hops for the hottest keys; invalidate L1 via pub/sub or keyspace notifications.
Use stale-while-revalidate: serve a stale value while refreshing asynchronously in the background, so readers never wait on a miss for hot keys that are within the grace window.

Implement probabilistic early expiration (XFetch/PER) for the hottest keys: independently roll dice to refresh before TTL fires, smearing recomputation across time instead of concentrating it at expiry.
Pre-warm the cache before scale-out events or deploys: run a priming script that touches the expected hot keys so new nodes do not start cold into rising traffic.
Version cache keys with a schema or payload prefix (e.g. product:v2:42) and bump the prefix on breaking changes so old entries age out instead of deserialising into wrong shapes.
sources: Cloud Design Patterns: Prescriptive Architecture Guidance for Cloud Applications (Microsoft patterns & practices, 2014) - Cache-Aside.

Scaling Memcache at Facebook (Nishtala et al., NSDI 2013) — introduces leases to prevent stale sets and thundering herds; peak DB query rate reduced from 17K/s to 1.3K/s for susceptible keys. https://www.usenix.org/conference/nsdi13/technical-sessions/presentation/nishtala

Performance at Scale with Amazon ElastiCache (AWS Whitepaper) — lazy caching as foundation, jittered TTLs, prewarming procedure, hot-key and hot-shard mitigation, combined lazy-loading + write-through hybrid guidance. https://docs.aws.amazon.com/pdfs/whitepapers/latest/scale-performance-elasticache/scale-performance-elasticache.pdf

AWS Caching Best Practices — TTL as blast-radius cap on bugs, combined lazy-loading + write-through, thundering herd effect, TTL jitter, cache prewarming, eviction policy selection (allkeys-lru vs allkeys-lfu). https://aws.amazon.com/caching/best-practices/

Redis Cache-Aside Guide (redis.io) — Go and Python implementations with Lua singleflight locks for stampede protection, stale-while-revalidate, explicit invalidation order (delete, never set). https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/use-cases/cache-aside/

"Optimal Probabilistic Cache Stampede Prevention" (Vattani, Chierichetti, Lowenstein, VLDB 2015) — XFetch/PER algorithm: refresh before TTL fires with probability rising as expiry approaches; lock-free, coordination-free stampede prevention at scale. https://www.vldb.org/pvls/vol14/p1357-vattani.pdf
